approach: The authors conducted a narrative review by synthesizing findings from preclinical studies (e.g., germ-free mouse models, antibiotic-treated models) and clinical trials/observational studies. They organized the material into thematic sections: 1) Clinical and preclinical evidence linking microbiota to ICB efficacy; 2) Mechanisms of action (metabolites, antigens, immune modulation); 3) Impact of adjuvant medications (antibiotics, steroids); 4) Therapeutic strategies (FMT, probiotics, diet, engineered bacteria). They utilized tables to summarize ongoing clinical trials and associations between specific bacteria and cancer types/prognosis.

contribution_and_limits.contribution: Provides a structured overview of the mechanistic links (metabolites, antigens) between gut microbiota and ICB efficacy. Summarizes a wide range of clinical trials testing microbiota-based adjuncts (FMT, probiotics, engineered bacteria). Highlights the potential of bacterial engineering and material science for next-generation therapies.
contribution_and_limits.limits: As a review, it does not present new primary experimental data. The causal relationships in humans are largely inferred from preclinical models and observational correlations. Variability in microbial signatures across different cancer types and cohorts is noted, limiting generalizability. The review acknowledges that many strategies are still in early-phase trials and safety/efficacy profiles are not fully established.

key_findings.finding: Germ-free status or broad-spectrum antibiotic use impairs ICB efficacy (anti-PD-1/PD-L1, anti-CTLA-4), reducing survival and tumor infiltration by CD8+ T cells.

Specific microbial signatures predict ICB response. Responders are often enriched with Akkermansia muciniphila, Bifidobacterium, Faecalibacterium, and Ruminococcaceae. Non-responders or those with poor prognosis may have higher levels of Fusobacterium nucleatum or Proteobacteria.

Microbial metabolites like SCFAs (butyrate, propionate) and indole derivatives regulate T-cell differentiation (Tregs vs. effector T cells) and checkpoint molecule expression. Microbial antigens activate dendritic cells and TLRs, promoting antitumor immunity.

FMT from ICB responders to non-responders can reverse resistance in some melanoma patients. Specific probiotics (e.g., Clostridium butyricum CBM588) combined with ICIs show improved response rates in renal cell carcinoma compared to ICI alone.
Antibiotics generally reduce ICB efficacy. Glucocorticoids (dexamethasone) may suppress beneficial microbes but also directly inhibit tumor immune evasion, showing dual effects.

problem_or_question: The review addresses the problem that many patients do not respond to or develop resistance against cancer immunotherapies, particularly ICIs. It seeks to understand the role of the gut microbiome in this variability and explores how manipulating the microbiome can enhance therapeutic outcomes and overcome resistance.
research_scope: The review focuses on the interaction between the gut microbiome and cancer immunotherapy, specifically immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). It covers preclinical models (germ-free mice), clinical observations in various cancer types (melanoma, colorectal cancer, lung cancer, renal cell carcinoma, etc.), and therapeutic strategies including fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), probiotics, dietary interventions, and engineered bacteria.
work_summary: This paper is a comprehensive review that synthesizes current knowledge on how the gut microbiome influences the efficacy of cancer immunotherapies. It begins by establishing the link between microbial composition and ICB response variability, highlighting specific bacterial signatures associated with responders versus non-responders. The review then details the mechanisms through which microbes modulate immunity, including metabolite production (SCFAs, indole derivatives) and antigen presentation. Finally, it evaluates emerging therapeutic strategies to harness this relationship, ranging from traditional FMT and probiotics to advanced synthetic biology approaches like engineered bacteria and bacterial derivatives, while also discussing challenges such as inter-individual variability and safety concerns.
